correctness.rationale: AB upper triangular has diagonal a_i b_i, so nilpotence iff each pair has zero product. Under nilpotence, its nilpotency index is n exactly when every first-superdiagonal entry N_{i,i+1}=a_i B_{i,i+1}+A_{i,i+1} b_{i+1} is nonzero; (N^(n-1))_{1n} is their product. L,R,Z diagonal state words allowing this are exactly L^j R^(n-j) or L^j Z R^(n-j-1). Their weighted count is (q-1)^(n-1)((n+1)q-1). Distinct superdiagonal tests use disjoint free coordinates and each has probability (q-1)/q. Multiplying by q^(n(n-1))(2q-1)^n nilpotent pairs proves the all-prime-power count. Independently enumerated n=2,q=2,3 and n=3,q=2 and all state words n<=6; finite work checks cases, not the proof.

originality.rationale: Sarma and Subedi derive the nilpotent-product event for a full upper triangular ring but do not refine by nilpotency index. Fuchs–Kirillov and Yip concern Jordan types for one uniformly sampled strictly triangular matrix, whose measure is different from the factorization-weighted product law. value.rationale: The highest-index Jordan stratum of a natural product distribution is a nontrivial probabilistic statistic; the simple closed all-n/q formula and contrasting fixed-q/large-q behavior are mathematically useful beyond the known probability of nilpotence.

final_claim: For independent uniform A,B in T_n(F_q), n>=2 and q any prime power, count of pairs with AB nilpotent of maximal index n is q^((n-1)^2)(q-1)^(2n-2)((n+1)q-1), with conditional nilpotent-product probability dividing by q^(n(n-1))(2q-1)^n.
limitations: Bounded independent experiments corroborate but do not replace the unrestricted analytic proof (or complete finite exhaustive argument for Pappus).
